new_statements.quote: In contrast, Bhaya has a variable stress position, which can change depending on the morphological foundation or sentence focus. Example: • Aer: "important"—/ˈɪm.pɔː.tənt/ (fixed initial stress) • Bhaya: "important" – /ɪmˈpɔː.tənt/ (variable stress placement) The stress on the initial syllable in Aer is predictable and unchanging, but in Bhaya, stress can shift to the subsequent syllable, especially in words with multiple sounds or lengthy morphological constructions.
new_statements.citation: Shafqat, Asmara, Javeria Ali Wadho & Nida Shabbir. 2025. Voices from the periphery: a constraint-based analysis of phonological variation in Sindhi's Aer and Bhaya endangered languages. Contemporary Journal of Social Science Review 3(3): 2353-2367. doi:10.63878/cjssr.v3i3.1259
new_statements.locator: sect. 4.3.1 'Stress Patterns', p. 2362 (abstract p. 2353: 'Aer exhibits fixed initial stress, whereas Bhaya allows for variable stress placement depending on the morphological structure')
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: statement check: other-problem. Opened the text we hold (aerr1238/ lines 542-566): the paper treats Aer and Bhaya as 'dialects of Sindhi', its only stress illustration is the English word 'important' transcribed two ways, and word- and sentence-level prominence are conflated; the 'variable stress' sentence exists but is not credible first-hand description of Bhaya word stress. Keep only as an unclear pointer. | checker: Held PDF+txt opened, 819 lines, pp. 2353-2367, title/authors/abstract as cited); Crossref record held by the project gives DOI 10.63878/cjssr.v3i3.1259, CJSSR 3(3):2353-2367, licence CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, VoR PDF link contemporaryjournal.com/index.php/14/article/download/1259/108…
new_statements.relation_note: States that Bhaya, unlike Aer (fixed initial stress), has variable stress placement depending on morphological structure or sentence focus, with stress able to shift to a later syllable; Praat pitch peaks 'moving depending on whether the syllable carried major stress'; sect. 4.3.3 calls Bhaya rhythm stress-timed. No placement rule, no native example.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Bhaya is described as variable (not fixed: initial syllable as in Aer), its position said to depend on morphological make-up or sentence focus and able to fall on a non-initial syllable; the source gives no rule locating it.
new_statements.identity_note: The article treats 'Aer and Bhaya' as two lesser-documented varieties of Sindhi 'spoken in the southeastern districts of Sindh', gives no ISO code, village or district and no wordforms other than English illustration words. The pairing Aer + Bhaya matches the SIL Sindh-survey/Ethnologue pair aeq + bhe (Bhaya: Kapri Goth near Samaro, Khipro, Jamesabad, Mirpurkhas; Aer: Jikrio Goth/Kunri, Jamesabad), and no other lect called Bhaya is known in Sindh, so identity with bhay1238 is probable but unproven. Quality caveats recorded by the Aer reader apply: stress and intonation 'examples' are English words, several cited references do not resolve in Crossref, low-tier venue. [name in source: Bhaya (a 'variety/dialect of Sindhi'); pages 2353 (abstract), 2357 (lit. review), 2362-2363 (sect. 4.3.1-4.3.3)]

sources.citation: Zubair, Saeed. 2016. A phonological description of Wadiyari, a language spoken in Pakistan. MA thesis, Payap University, Chiang Mai. xvi+187 pp. (ch. 2 'previous language surveys in Sindh': sect. 2.3.1 Grainger & Grainger 1980, sect. 2.3.2 Jeffery (ed.) 1999 'Sindh Survey Month', sect. 2.5 + Fig. 14 classification of the languages of Sindh)
sources.note: Nothing for Bhaya. The only prosodic remark in the survey chapter (p. 15: Grainger & Grainger 1980: 48 'none of the languages has phonemic word or syllable-tone'; stress not marked, assumed predictable) concerns Grainger's 20 varieties, and p. 16 states Bhaya, Ghera, Goaria, Gurgula and Jandavra 'were not reported previously, not even in Grainger & Grainger (1980)', so that group-level statement does not extend to them.

sources.citation: Grimes, Barbara F. (ed.) 2000. Ethnologue: Languages of the World, 14th edition. Dallas: SIL International. Entry 'BHAYA [BHE]' (web version, Internet Archive copy 2003).
sources.note: Nothing. Entry gives population 70-700 (1998), Lower Sindh locations (Kapri Goth near Samaro, Khipro, Jamesabad, Mirpurkhas, Phuladia, Hyderabad), a key-morpheme note (possessive postposition in g-, Rajasthani-type gender endings, possible identity with Bhoyari of India) and lexical-similarity percentages from an unpublished 1998 SIL Sindh survey; no phonology.
